fate: Taken private by a CITIC Capital-led group, 2014 (~$890M, as AsiaInfo-Linkage)
dek: AsiaInfo built the networks and billing software that brought China's state phone companies onto the internet.
lede: A small company started by Chinese students who had studied in America ended up building the internet backbones of China's state phone carriers. That company was AsiaInfo. It turned imported routers into working national networks, then wrote the software that ran them and sent the bills. When AsiaInfo filed to go public in early 2000, China had only a few million people online. Investors were hungry for any way to own a piece of what came next.

sections.heading: Roads Made of Routers
sections.body: The founders bet that China would build its internet the way it built roads: fast, at national scale, and through a few big state carriers. Those carriers had money and a mandate. They had little experience with routers, network design, or customer billing. AsiaInfo set out to be the systems integrator in the middle. It turned imported hardware into working networks, and later it wrote the operations and billing software that kept them running.

sections.heading: A Tripled Debut, Then CITIC
sections.body: AsiaInfo priced at $24 a share in March 2000 and more than tripled on its first day. It was one of the last great openings before the dot-com peak broke. Over the next decade the company moved from building networks to selling telecom software. In 2010 it merged with Linkage Technologies to form AsiaInfo-Linkage. In 2014 a group led by CITIC Capital, including co-founder Edward Tian, took it private.

cover.theme: a Chinese mountain landscape scroll (a vast country, slowly connected)

tagline: The Land Rush for Dot-Com Names
dek: Register.com made it easy for small businesses and ordinary people to claim a web address of their own.
lede: Register.com was one of the first companies allowed to compete with Network Solutions for .com names. Owning a .com then felt like owning land in a city still being drawn. Register.com made claiming that land simple for small businesses and ordinary people, and it moved fast. When it filed to go public in early 2000, people were claiming millions of new names every year. The land rush looked like it might never end.

sections.heading: Front Door to the Web
sections.body: The Forman brothers started out running an internet service business in New York. They saw that the hardest step for most customers was the first one: getting a name. When the domain registry opened to competition, they made a bet. A clean, fast storefront for names could become the front door to everything else a small business needed online, from email to hosting to a basic website.

sections.heading: Cheaper Names, $7.81 a Share
sections.body: Register.com priced at $24 a share in March 2000. Competition among registrars soon drove name prices down. The company spent the next years leaning on add-on services to keep its customers. Richard Forman stepped down as chief executive in 2003. In 2005, Vector Capital agreed to buy Register.com for $7.81 a share in cash, a deal worth about $200 million.

cover.theme: a city street of addresses (domain names)

dek: Onvia showed small businesses which government agencies were buying what, so they could win public contracts.
lede: Onvia's most valuable product turned out to be a list: which government agencies were buying what, and when. It did not start that way. Onvia began in Seattle as a one-stop online shop for firms too small to have a purchasing department. By the time it filed to go public in early 2000, it was also pointing those firms toward government. Agencies spent huge sums every year, and finding the right bid took luck and paperwork.

sections.heading: A Young Canadian's Marketplace
sections.body: Glenn Ballman, a young Canadian entrepreneur, founded the company in 1996. He bet that the web served small businesses badly, and that they would gather in one place if someone made buying and selling easier. Over time the most valuable part of that idea was information. If a small firm knew which agencies were buying what, and when, it could compete for public contracts.

sections.heading: From Store to Bid Tracker
sections.body: Onvia priced at $21 a share in March 2000, just before the dot-com market turned. The broad small-business marketplace did not survive the downturn. The company narrowed its focus to government purchasing data. It spent nearly two decades as a smaller public company selling that intelligence. In 2017 Deltek bought Onvia for $9 a share, about $70 million, and folded it into its GovWin service.

cover.theme: a county courthouse (small business meets government)
cover.artwork: Fairfax Court House, Virginia, with Union Soldiers in Front and on the Roof

dek: Niku let consulting firms and IT departments see every project, person and billable hour in one place.
lede: Factories had measured every hour of work for generations. Offices mostly had not. Consulting firms, IT departments and service businesses ran on people's time, and most tracked it in spreadsheets. Niku sold one system to plan, staff and bill those projects. When it filed to go public in early 2000, enterprise software was booming. A single system for knowledge work sounded like the next big software category.

sections.heading: A Second Act After Diba
sections.body: Farzad Dibachi co-founded Niku in 1998, after selling his earlier company, Diba, to Sun Microsystems. He bet that service firms needed their own version of the planning systems manufacturers already used. If a firm could see every project, every person and every hour in one place, it could price work better. It could staff jobs faster. It could stop losing money on work it had already won.

sections.heading: Smaller, Then Sold to CA
sections.body: Niku priced at $24 a share in February 2000 and traded far higher in its first months. The crash that followed hit the company hard. It spent several years cutting costs and narrowing its focus to IT governance and project portfolio software. The narrower product found steady buyers. In 2005 Computer Associates agreed to buy Niku for $21 a share in cash, about $350 million.

cover.theme: scaffolding around a building (projects under construction)

dek: VarsityBooks sold college students their textbooks online for less than the campus bookstore charged.
lede: Every semester, college students stood in long lines at the campus bookstore and paid full price for books they would use for four months. VarsityBooks.com wanted them to order from a laptop instead, at a discount. When it filed to go public at the start of 2000, online retail was the hottest story in business. A captive audience of wired students looked like an easy win.

sections.heading: Cheaper Books Before Class
sections.body: The company bet that students would gladly order textbooks online if the price was lower and the books arrived before class. It promised discounts off list price and fast shipping. It spent heavily on campus marketing to build the brand. The deeper idea was about the campus bookstore, which convenience had protected for decades. Once ordering online became just as easy, that hold would break.

sections.heading: Running the Bookstores Instead
sections.body: VarsityBooks priced at $10 a share in February 2000. Deep discounts proved hard to keep up. The company changed course and renamed itself Varsity Group. It began running online bookstores for schools instead of competing with them, and it built a modest business serving private high schools and colleges. In 2008 Follett, the big bookstore operator, bought the company for a fraction of its offering price.

cover.theme: a reader with a book (study without the campus line)

dek: LendingTree let borrowers fill out one loan form online and watch several lenders bid for their business.
lede: Getting a mortgage used to mean visiting banks one by one and hoping the first offer was fair. LendingTree flipped that. A borrower filled out one form, and lenders bid for the loan. When the company filed to go public in early 2000, shopping for lenders from a kitchen table was a new idea. Its slogan said it plainly: when banks compete, you win.

sections.heading: A Banking Town Upstart
sections.body: Doug Lebda founded the company in 1996 in Charlotte, a banking city. His bet was that the internet could flip the loan process. Instead of borrowers chasing banks, lenders would compete for borrowers. LendingTree did not lend money itself. It earned fees from lenders for qualified requests. That let it grow without holding any loans on its own balance sheet.

sections.heading: IAC and Back Again
sections.body: LendingTree priced at $12 a share in February 2000. It grew through the housing boom, and in 2003 IAC bought the company. In 2008, in the middle of the financial crisis, IAC spun it back out as a separate public company, and Lebda returned to lead it. The business grew from mortgages into credit cards, personal loans and insurance. It still trades on Nasdaq under its original ticker, TREE.

cover.theme: an apple tree (the lending tree)

dek: Savvis gave banks and big companies faster, more reliable connections than the public internet, plus data centers for their servers.
lede: Banks and trading firms could not afford to wait in the public internet's traffic jams. Savvis sold them a way around: private networks and data centers that carried business traffic out of sight. When Savvis filed to go public in early 2000, it was closely tied to Bridge Information Systems, a financial data company. Many investors thought infrastructure was the safest place to put internet money.

sections.heading: Skipping the Crowded Exchanges
sections.body: Savvis bet that businesses would pay a premium for a managed network that avoided the congested public exchange points. It routed traffic over its own backbone. It ran the data centers where customers placed their servers. The business needed a lot of capital up front. It rested on one assumption: demand for bandwidth and hosting would rise fast enough to fill all that capacity.

sections.heading: Surviving Bridge's Collapse
sections.body: Savvis priced at $24 a share in February 2000. The telecom bust that followed nearly broke it. Then Bridge went bankrupt in 2001 and added more strain. Savvis survived. It bought assets from failed rivals and grew into a major hosting and early cloud provider. In 2011 CenturyLink bought the company in a deal worth about $3.2 billion, including debt.

cover.theme: a factory chimney under construction (industrial infrastructure)

fate: Sold its businesses to Claranet and Interoute, 2005
dek: VIA NET.WORKS bought small internet providers in Europe and Latin America to serve small businesses under one name.
lede: Much of Europe's business internet access once came from small local providers, each with a few thousand customers. VIA NET.WORKS set out to buy many of them and join them under one name. When it filed to go public in early 2000, the plan sounded simple. Buy cheaply. Share costs. Sell more services to small and mid-sized firms across many countries.

sections.heading: Many Shops, One Back Office
sections.body: The bet was a roll-up. Local providers had loyal customers and local knowledge, but little scale. By buying them and combining their back offices, VIA hoped to sell hosting, connectivity and other services more cheaply than any single provider could. It bought firms in several European countries and in Latin America. The goal was to become the default internet partner for small businesses.

sections.heading: Sold Off in Pieces
sections.body: VIA priced at $21 a share in February 2000. Joining so many small companies together proved hard, and the market for internet stocks collapsed soon after the offering. The company spent the next years selling units, cutting costs and looking for a buyer. In 2005 it sold most of its operations. Claranet took one part, and Interoute took the rest.

cover.theme: travelers on the road (all roads lead online)

dek: eMerge tried to move the American cattle trade online, then turned to tracking how beef was raised.
lede: eMerge Interactive's revenue passed a billion dollars in 2001, thanks to the cattle brokers it had bought. The company had set out to move a trade run on sale barns, brokers and handshakes onto the internet. It was a spinout of the incubator XL Vision. When it filed to go public in early 2000, business-to-business marketplaces were the newest craze. Few markets looked as big or as old-fashioned as American beef.

sections.heading: From Imaging to Feedlots
sections.body: eMerge began as an imaging technology company before it turned to agriculture. Its bet was that an online marketplace and better data could make the cattle trade work better for ranchers, feedlots and packers. The company bought cattle brokers to bring volume onto its system. It also built tools to track animals and verify how beef was raised and handled. The industry it chose ran on trust and long relationships.

sections.heading: Trading Out, Tracking In
sections.body: eMerge priced at $15 a share in February 2000. Buying brokerage firms pushed revenue past a billion dollars in 2001, but the trading business lost large sums. In 2002 the company decided to exit cattle operations. It focused instead on CattleLog, a verification program, and VerifEYE, a meat inspection technology. Weak beef markets after the 2003 mad cow scare made that path hard too.

cover.theme: a bull (the cattle trade)

dek: FirePond let buyers and salespeople configure complex machines online and get an accurate price and quote.
lede: A truck, a tractor or an industrial machine could come with thousands of options, and many of them did not work together. FirePond made the software that kept those choices straight. A salesperson, or a buyer on the web, could configure a product, see a price and get a valid quote. When FirePond filed to go public in early 2000, companies were rushing to move their sales online.

sections.heading: A Minnesota Tool Goes Online
sections.body: FirePond grew out of an older Minnesota company that built configuration tools for manufacturers. It bet that the web would turn this back-office tool into a front-door one. If customers could configure and price their own orders online, manufacturers could sell more and make fewer mistakes. They could also spend less on the long back-and-forth of complex sales. FirePond already had paying customers when it filed.

sections.heading: $3.16 a Share in Cash
sections.body: FirePond priced at $22 a share in February 2000, weeks before the Nasdaq peaked. Spending on e-business software fell steeply the next year. The company cut staff and faced shareholder lawsuits from the offering period. In 2003 an affiliate of Jaguar Technology Holdings bought FirePond for $3.16 a share in cash, about $11.7 million. Its run as a public company lasted less than four years.

cover.theme: fireworks over dark water (fire on a pond)
cover.artwork: Fire Works on the Night of the Fourth of July

dek: Centra let companies teach and meet live over the internet, so employees could learn from their own desks.
lede: Corporate training in the 1990s usually meant flying employees to a hotel ballroom. Centra offered a virtual classroom instead. An instructor could speak, show slides and take questions from people sitting at their own desks. When Centra filed to go public in early 2000, e-learning was a hot category. Live teaching over ordinary internet connections still felt almost like science fiction.

sections.heading: Slides Over Slow Lines
sections.body: Leon Navickas founded Centra near Boston in 1995. He bet that live, interactive learning could work over the internet if the software handled voice, slides and participation well on slow connections. Companies spent large sums flying people to training. Centra argued it could cut those costs and reach more employees, more often, wherever they were. Most of its customers were big companies with staff spread across many offices.

sections.heading: Folded Into Saba
sections.body: Centra priced at $14 a share in February 2000. It kept building its virtual classroom and meeting tools through the downturn. It also faced growing competition from web conferencing firms with simpler products. In 2006 the learning software company Saba bought Centra in a deal worth about $60 million. Years later, live online classes became an everyday part of work and school.

cover.theme: a lecture in progress (the classroom, moved online)

dek: Turnstone made gear that let phone carriers connect and test DSL lines remotely instead of sending a technician.
lede: Every new DSL line had to be connected and tested by hand, in crowded phone company central offices. Turnstone Systems built equipment that did that work remotely. Phone companies and their new rivals were racing to sell DSL, broadband delivered over old copper phone lines. When Turnstone filed to go public at the start of 2000, DSL was spreading fast. Its customers were raising money at a remarkable pace.

sections.heading: The Central Office Bottleneck
sections.body: Turnstone bet that the DSL boom would create a bottleneck in the central office, where technicians had to connect and test each copper line. Its equipment let carriers switch and test lines from afar, which saved truck rolls and time. Many of its biggest customers were the competitive local carriers born after the Telecommunications Act of 1996. Turnstone's fortunes rose and fell with theirs.

sections.heading: Wound Down, Cash Returned
sections.body: Turnstone priced at $29 a share in February 2000, and investors valued it richly at first. Within a year, many of the young DSL carriers it served ran out of money and failed. Much of Turnstone's demand went with them. The company chose to wind down instead of chasing a shrinking market. Shareholders approved a liquidation, and Turnstone returned its remaining cash in a series of payouts.

cover.theme: shorebirds over moonlit waves (the turnstone)

dek: Neoforma moved hospital buying online, so hospitals could order supplies and equipment with less paper and fewer calls.
lede: Hospitals buy everything from gauze to imaging machines, mostly through paper orders, phone calls and group contracts. Neoforma set out to move all of it online. When it filed to go public in early 2000, health care was one of the biggest markets the internet had not yet touched. Business-to-business exchanges were promising to strip cost out of entire industries, and Neoforma wanted to be health care's exchange.

sections.heading: Partners Who Became Owners
sections.body: Neoforma began in 1996 as a way for hospitals to find medical equipment. The bet grew larger: hospitals, suppliers and distributors would all meet on one electronic exchange. The company signed long agreements with VHA and University HealthSystem Consortium, two big hospital purchasing groups. Those deals brought hospitals onto the system. They also made the two groups major shareholders and tied Neoforma closely to two customers.

sections.heading: Absorbed by GHX
sections.body: Neoforma priced at $13 a share in January 2000 and soared in its first months. The broad exchange idea faded with the market. The company settled into selling purchasing software and data services to its partner hospitals. In 2006 Global Healthcare Exchange, a rival backed by the industry, completed its purchase of Neoforma in a deal worth about $200 million. Neoforma's software lived on inside the larger exchange.

cover.theme: a field hospital (medical supply at scale)
cover.artwork: Field Hospital, Second Army Corps, Brandy Station

tagline: Product Catalogs Ready for the Web
dek: OnDisplay gathered product details from scattered supplier catalogs so online stores could show accurate items and prices.
lede: A store cannot sell what it cannot describe. Online stores had a basic problem: the product details they needed lived in dozens of places, in different formats, owned by different suppliers. OnDisplay made software that gathered that content and got it ready for the web. When it filed to go public in late 1999, e-commerce sites were multiplying. Every one of them needed something to put in the window.

sections.heading: Catalogs on Paper and Spreadsheets
sections.body: OnDisplay bet that content integration would become a core layer of online commerce. Suppliers kept their catalogs in databases, spreadsheets and paper. Without help, each site had to clean up every supplier's data on its own. OnDisplay's software pulled that information together, cleaned it, and kept it current. Retailers and marketplaces could then show accurate products and prices without rebuilding their own systems.

sections.heading: $1.7 Billion in Vignette Stock
sections.body: OnDisplay priced at $28 a share in December 1999 and rose quickly in the last rush of the dot-com market. It did not stay independent for long. In 2000 Vignette, the content management company, agreed to buy OnDisplay in an all-stock deal worth about $1.7 billion when it was announced. Later that year the market collapsed, and the value of that stock fell sharply.

cover.theme: a print-shop window (goods on display)

dek: GRIC let business travelers dial into the internet abroad through local providers and get one bill at home.
lede: Before Wi-Fi was everywhere, a business traveler who wanted email abroad had to find a local dial-up number or pay for an expensive call home. GRIC built an alliance of internet providers around the world so their customers could log on through one another. When it filed to go public in late 1999, mobile workers were multiplying. Laptops were becoming standard business equipment.

sections.heading: Roaming, Borrowed From Phones
sections.body: GRIC bet that the internet needed roaming, the way mobile phones did. It signed up providers in many countries and handled the settlement between them. A customer of one provider could log on through another and get billed at home. Small providers could offer global reach without building networks abroad. GRIC sat in the middle as the clearing house, and it earned a share of each connection.

sections.heading: GoRemote, Then iPass
sections.body: GRIC priced at $14 a share in December 1999. As corporate laptops spread, the company shifted from serving internet providers to selling remote access directly to big companies. Its customers were mostly large firms with traveling staff. It renamed itself GoRemote Internet Communications in 2004. The larger rival iPass had long chased the same travelers. In 2006 iPass completed an all-cash purchase of GoRemote worth about $76.5 million.

cover.theme: a map of the world and its tradewinds (dial in from anywhere)

tagline: Online Degrees Under the College's Name
dek: eCollege ran the technology behind colleges' online degree programs, so schools could teach online without building it.
lede: eCollege often took a share of the tuition from the online courses it ran, while the college's name stayed on the door. Founded in Denver as Real Education, it offered to build and run internet courses for schools that had no idea how. When it filed to go public at the end of 1999, online learning was a promising experiment. Earning a degree without stepping on campus still struck many people as strange.

sections.heading: The Quiet Partner
sections.body: A few colleges had begun to offer whole courses over the internet, and eCollege wanted the rest. It bet that colleges would want to reach students online without building the technology themselves. It supplied the course platform, hosting and support. In many cases it shared in the tuition revenue from online programs. The college focused on teaching, and eCollege kept the systems running behind the school's brand.

sections.heading: $22.45 a Share From Pearson
sections.body: eCollege priced at $11 a share in December 1999. Its shares fell with the market, but its business grew as online degree programs spread, especially at for-profit and continuing education schools. The company also bought Datamark, a marketing services firm. In 2007 Pearson agreed to buy eCollege for $22.45 a share, about $538 million, to build out its digital education business.

cover.theme: a college library (the campus, moved online)

tagline: The Web's Version of TV Ratings
dek: NetRatings told advertisers who was actually visiting websites, using a panel of tracked internet users.
lede: Television had Nielsen ratings. The web had a flood of traffic claims and almost no numbers anyone trusted. NetRatings built a panel of internet users, measured their browsing, and sold the results to publishers and advertisers. When it filed to go public in late 1999, online ad spending was soaring. Buyers badly wanted to know who was actually watching, and NetRatings promised to tell them.

sections.heading: Borrowing Nielsen's Name
sections.body: NetRatings bet that the internet would need an independent ratings service, just as broadcasting had. Advertisers would not move big budgets online without audience numbers they believed. Early on, NetRatings formed a partnership with Nielsen Media Research, which lent its data a name advertisers already trusted. The service became known as Nielsen//NetRatings. Its numbers became a common currency in online advertising.

sections.heading: Bought Back by Nielsen
sections.body: NetRatings priced at $17 a share in December 1999. After the crash it bought several rivals and research firms as the market consolidated. It stayed one of the standard sources for web audience data, and Nielsen held a large stake throughout. In 2007 Nielsen bought the shares it did not already own for $21 each, in a deal worth about $327 million.

cover.theme: a theatre audience (counting who is watching)
cover.artwork: Audience at a Parisian Theatre I

fate: Taken private by Omnicom-backed Seneca Investments, 2001
tagline: A Web Shop Priced Like the Web
dek: Agency.com built websites and online campaigns for big brands that were still working out what the web was for.
lede: Interactive agencies were among the hottest stocks on the market in 1999, valued less like ad firms and more like the internet itself. Agency.com was one of the New York shops behind that craze. It built websites and online campaigns for major brands that had only just started thinking about the web. When it filed to go public in late 1999, one of its early backers was Omnicom, the advertising giant.

sections.heading: Design, Code and Marketing
sections.body: Chan Suh and Kyle Shannon founded Agency.com in 1995, when few big companies had a website. They bet the web would need its own kind of agency, one that mixed design, technology and marketing in a way traditional ad firms could not. Omnicom invested early. The agency grew fast by winning big corporate clients and buying smaller interactive shops in the United States and Europe.

sections.heading: $3.35 and Back to Omnicom
sections.body: Agency.com priced at $26 a share in December 1999, at the height of the interactive agency craze. When the dot-com market fell, corporate budgets for websites fell with it. In 2001 Seneca Investments, a vehicle formed by Omnicom and Pegasus Partners, took the agency private for $3.35 a share. It ran for years inside the Omnicom family before it merged into TBWA.

cover.theme: a Paris cabaret poster (advertising as art)

dek: Harris Interactive moved the famous Harris Poll from the telephone to the internet, asking millions of people online.
lede: For decades, polling meant calling people at home during dinner. Harris Interactive, owner of the famous Harris Poll, bet that the internet could do it faster, cheaper and at far larger scale. By the time it filed to go public in late 1999, it had built a panel of millions of people willing to answer surveys online. The polling industry was watching to see if the method would hold up.

sections.heading: Buying the Harris Poll
sections.body: Gordon Black founded his research firm in Rochester in 1975. Later he bought Louis Harris and Associates, the pollster behind the Harris Poll. His bet was that online panels could replace telephone surveys for much of market research. Online surveys cost less, could show images and video, and could reach thousands of people in days instead of weeks. It was a bold move for a firm with a famous brand to protect.

sections.heading: Elections, Then $2 a Share
sections.body: Harris Interactive priced at $14 a share in December 1999. Many people doubted its online polls at first. Then the polls performed well in several elections, and internet research went mainstream. Over time, cheaper online survey tools pushed prices down, and the company lost money for several years. In 2014 Nielsen completed its purchase of Harris Interactive for $2 a share, about $117 million.

cover.theme: a holiday crowd at a temple fair (public opinion)
cover.artwork: Crowds at the Year-end Fair at Kinryuzan Temple in Asakusa (Asakusa Kinryuzan toshi no ichi gunshu), from the series "Famous Places in the Eastern Capital (Toto meisho)"

dek: PFSweb packed, shipped and answered customer calls for brands selling online, so they did not need their own warehouses.
lede: Behind every online store sit warehouses, pick lists, shipping labels, returns and call centers. PFSweb offered to run all of it. The company was spun out of Daisytek, a distributor of computer supplies, and it sold that know-how to brands that wanted to sell directly on the web. When it filed to go public in late 1999, retailers and manufacturers were rushing online without knowing how they would deliver.

sections.heading: Daisytek's Warehouse Skills, for Rent
sections.body: PFSweb bet that many companies would want to sell online without building their own fulfillment operations. It took over the work after the click. It processed orders, stored goods, packed and shipped them, handled payments, and answered customer calls. That gave a brand one partner for the whole chain, from the warehouse shelf to the customer's phone call. It brought its parent's logistics experience to brands that had never shipped single orders to consumers.

sections.heading: Two Decades, Then GXO
sections.body: PFSweb priced at $17 a share in December 1999. Its shares fell with the market, but the business it chose lasted as e-commerce kept growing. It served brands in fashion, health and consumer goods. For a time it also ran an e-commerce agency. It stayed public for more than two decades. In 2023 the logistics company GXO bought PFSweb and added its fulfillment network to GXO's own.

cover.theme: a harbor dock (goods shipped out)
cover.artwork: The New Dock at la Rochelle

dek: Digital Impact sent personalized emails to millions of shoppers for big retailers, and measured what brought them back.
lede: Email was becoming the most direct way a company could reach its customers, and the most abused. Digital Impact gave big brands a professional way to do it: personalized messages, sent by the million, with tracking to show what worked. When it filed to go public in late 1999, online retailers were building customer lists fast. They wanted a way to bring shoppers back for a second order.

sections.heading: Millions of Messages, Measured
sections.body: Digital Impact bet that email would become a core marketing channel for big companies, and that they would hire specialists to run it. It built systems to send millions of personalized messages, track opens and clicks, and tune campaigns. It sold mainly to big retailers and consumer brands. It pitched itself as a full-service partner, a step beyond a simple tool for sending mail.

sections.heading: InfoUSA Bids, Acxiom Wins
sections.body: Digital Impact priced at $15 a share in November 1999. Its shares fell with the internet market. Email marketing grew more crowded and cheaper over time. The company kept its focus on big brands and expanded into broader marketing services. It stayed public for more than five years. In 2005, after an unsolicited bid from InfoUSA, the data company Acxiom agreed to buy Digital Impact for about $140 million.

cover.theme: a beauty reading a letter (email)

dek: deltathree carried phone calls over the internet and charged far less than traditional long distance carriers.
lede: An international phone call could cost dollars a minute when deltathree started sending calls over the internet for far less. It was one of the first companies to try. RSL Communications controlled deltathree when it filed to go public in late 1999. Internet telephony was still crackly and new. The long distance carriers were only starting to worry about it.

sections.heading: Voice as Data Packets
sections.body: deltathree bet that voice would become just another kind of internet traffic. It turned calls into data packets and routed them over a network it built for the job, so it did not rely only on the public internet. That let it undercut traditional carriers, especially on international routes. It sold to consumers through a product that let a PC call a phone. It also sold cheap capacity to other carriers and businesses.

sections.heading: Undercut by Skype
sections.body: deltathree priced at $15 a share in November 1999. Internet calling did take off, but prices fell to almost nothing, and bigger players such as Skype changed the market. deltathree shrank over the next decade. In 2009 D4 Holdings, an investment fund linked to the owners of ACN, bought a controlling stake. By then deltathree was a small company carrying heavy losses.

cover.theme: water carriers on the Nile (traffic flowing down a river delta)

tagline: The Ad Agency That Ran on MOJO
dek: Mediaplex gave advertisers software to choose which online ad each person saw, and proof of what worked.
lede: Within months of going public, Mediaplex was worth billions on a simple promise: software could decide which ad each person saw. Early web ads were mostly banners bought by hand and measured loosely. The San Francisco company offered real machinery to pick the ad, the moment and the viewer, then measure the result. When it filed in late 1999, internet ad spending was rising fast, and marketers wanted proof the money worked.

sections.heading: Agency Meets Ad Server
sections.body: Gregory Raifman founded Mediaplex in San Francisco in 1996. He bet that online advertising would come to run on data and software, with messages that changed based on the viewer and the moment. Mediaplex paired the services of an agency with its own ad-serving technology, called MOJO. Clients could use it to run complex campaigns across many sites at once.

sections.heading: Folded Into ValueClick
sections.body: Mediaplex priced at $12 a share in November 1999. Then the online ad market collapsed in 2000 and 2001, and many of its dot-com clients disappeared with it. In 2001 ValueClick bought Mediaplex in a stock deal, two years after the offering. Raifman stayed on the ValueClick board into 2002. The Mediaplex ad-serving technology lived on inside ValueClick for years after the merger.

cover.theme: street advertising posters (the ad, placed where people look)

fate: Taken private by Thoma Bravo, 2010; acquired by Dell, 2012; independent again since 2016
tagline: A Firewall in a Small Box
dek: SonicWALL sold small businesses an affordable firewall box that kept intruders off their newly connected networks.
lede: SonicWALL began as Sonic Systems, a maker of networking products for Apple computers. It made its name with a different box. Small offices, newly connected by DSL and cable modems, had almost no protection. SonicWALL sold them a firewall appliance that sat between their network and the internet and kept intruders out. When it filed to go public in late 1999, always-on broadband was spreading fast, and so were the attacks.

sections.heading: Two Brothers and Their Resellers
sections.body: The brothers Sreekanth and Sudhakar Ravi started the company in 1991. Big companies had security teams and expensive firewalls. The brothers bet that small businesses would pay for real security too, if it came as a simple appliance at an affordable price. SonicWALL sold through resellers who installed and supported the boxes for local customers. That reseller network became one of its biggest strengths.

sections.heading: Thoma Bravo, Dell, and Back
sections.body: SonicWALL priced at $14 a share in November 1999. It survived the downturn and stayed public for a decade. Through those years, its brand and its focus on smaller customers stayed largely the same. In 2010 Thoma Bravo took it private, and in 2012 Dell bought it. In 2016 Dell sold its software businesses, and SonicWALL became independent again under private equity owners.

cover.theme: a fortress above a walled town (a wall that keeps intruders out)
cover.artwork: View of Pirna with the Fortress of Sonnenstein

dek: Tickets.com sold event tickets online and gave venues their own ticketing systems, as an alternative to Ticketmaster.
lede: Tickets.com picked a fight with Ticketmaster and ended up owned by Major League Baseball. Buying a concert or ball game ticket then meant a phone line, a box office or an outlet in a record store. Tickets.com put the sale online and gave venues their own ticketing systems. When it filed to go public in late 1999, it promised fans an easier way to buy. It promised venues a choice beyond the dominant player.

sections.heading: Venues That Wanted Control
sections.body: Tickets.com bet that the internet could break the hold of a single ticketing giant. It combined several ticketing software companies. It offered venues technology they could run themselves, plus online sales. It worked with theaters, arts centers and sports teams, and many of them wanted more control over their customers and their fees. The fight was hard, because the market leader held long exclusive contracts with many big venues.

sections.heading: Bought by Baseball for $1.10
sections.body: Tickets.com priced at $12.50 a share in November 1999. It lost money for years fighting a much bigger rival, and its stock fell far below the offering price. Its strongest ties turned out to be with baseball teams. In 2005 Major League Baseball Advanced Media bought the company for $1.10 a share, about $66 million. The league used it to build its own ticketing for clubs across baseball.

cover.theme: a theatre box (a ticket to the show)
cover.artwork: The Loge with the Gilded Mask

dek: Akamai made websites load faster by serving each visitor from a nearby server in a worldwide network.
lede: Akamai's stock closed its first day above $145, more than five times its offering price, on the strength of an idea from MIT. Popular websites often slowed to a crawl or crashed under heavy traffic. Akamai, named for the Hawaiian word for smart, copied content to thousands of servers around the world and served each visitor from the nearest one. People had a name for the problem: the World Wide Wait.

sections.heading: An Algorithm From MIT
sections.body: MIT professor Tom Leighton and graduate student Danny Lewin bet that clever algorithms could fix internet congestion without rebuilding the internet. Their system decided, in real time, which server should answer each request. One origin server no longer had to strain under all the demand. The load spread across a global network placed inside many internet providers, close to the people asking for content.

sections.heading: September 11, and Beyond
sections.body: Akamai priced at $26 a share in October 1999 and soared on its first day, one of the great debuts of the era. The crash cut its value sharply. On September 11, 2001, Danny Lewin was killed aboard American Airlines Flight 11. The company survived and grew into a core part of the internet's infrastructure and security. It still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker AKAM.

cover.theme: a great Pacific wave (Akamai, Hawaiian for smart; traffic surging at the edge)
cover.artwork: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Kanagawa oki nami ura), also known as The Great Wave, from the series "Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji (Fugaku sanjūrokkei)"

fate: Still public as Gaia, Inc. (NASDAQ: GAIA) after selling its consumer brands
dek: Gaiam sold yoga gear, eco-friendly goods and wellness videos to people who wanted to live healthier and greener.
lede: Gaiam took its name from Gaia, the Greek goddess of the Earth. It sold to a group marketers had begun to call cultural creatives: people who cared about health, the environment and personal growth. Through catalogs, the web and stores, it offered yoga mats, organic goods and wellness videos. When it filed to go public in late 1999, Gaiam was one of the few lifestyle brands built around a set of values.

sections.heading: From Corporate Express to Yoga
sections.body: Jirka Rysavy, who also founded the office supply company Corporate Express, started Gaiam in 1988. He bet that enough shoppers wanted products that matched their values, and that one company could serve them across many categories. Gaiam paired direct sales with media. Its fitness and yoga videos were products in their own right. They also drew customers to everything else Gaiam sold.

sections.heading: Sold the Mats, Kept Streaming
sections.body: Gaiam priced at $5 a share in October 1999, a modest offering in a frothy year. It grew into a well-known yoga and fitness brand sold in big retail chains. Over time its two halves pulled apart. In 2016 it sold the Gaiam consumer brand business and kept its streaming video service. It renamed itself Gaia. Gaia still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker GAIA.

cover.theme: a quiet forest interior (Gaia, the living earth)
cover.artwork: A Forest Interior, with a Seated Figure

dek: Sycamore made optical switches that let carriers set up fiber connections in minutes through software.
lede: Sycamore Networks closed its first trading day above $184 a share, which gave a year-old company a market value in the tens of billions. Carriers were laying fiber as fast as they could, sure that internet traffic would double every few months. Sycamore promised to make that fiber smarter. Its optical switches could set up and change high-speed connections through software instead of by hand. Few companies captured the fiber dream so completely.

sections.heading: The Cascade Team, Again
sections.body: Desh Deshpande and Daniel Smith, who had built Cascade Communications together, founded Sycamore in 1998. They bet that optical networks needed intelligence. Carriers then configured fixed connections over weeks. With Sycamore's switches, they could provision bandwidth in minutes. That promised to turn raw fiber into a flexible service and to save carriers large sums in equipment and labor. Carriers lined up to try it.

sections.heading: Cash Outlasts the Customers
sections.body: Sycamore priced at $38 a share in October 1999 and soared on its first day. When the telecom bubble burst, carrier spending collapsed, and Sycamore's sales collapsed with it. The money it had raised in the boom kept it alive long after its customers stopped buying. The company held large cash reserves for years. In 2013 it sold its remaining business and began to dissolve, returning cash to shareholders.

cover.theme: a single sycamore tree

dek: NaviSite ran the servers behind other companies' websites and applications from its own data centers.
lede: NaviSite began as the in-house hosting shop for CMGI, the internet holding company, and then sold the same service to everyone else. Every company wanted a website, and few wanted to run the servers behind it. NaviSite hosted and managed those sites in its own data centers. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, hosting looked like a way to profit from the web without betting on any single website.

sections.heading: Rent, Don't Build
sections.body: NaviSite's bet was that its hosting skill could become a business of its own. Outside customers needed reliable, managed hosting. They could rent space, bandwidth and expertise instead of building data centers, and NaviSite would earn steady monthly fees. CMGI's own family of internet companies gave it a base of customers from the start. Each new site meant another rack of servers and another monthly bill.

sections.heading: Bought by Time Warner Cable
sections.body: NaviSite priced at $14 a share in October 1999. Its dot-com customers vanished in the crash. The company went through years of losses, restructuring and acquisitions. It slowly shifted toward managed services and application hosting for bigger businesses. In 2011 Time Warner Cable bought NaviSite for about $230 million to grow its business services. The deal came more than eleven years after the offering.

cover.theme: a sailing ship (navigation)
cover.artwork: British Sail Ship, from the set of eight Pictures of Foreign Ships

dek: Interwoven let big teams write, review and publish a company's website together without breaking it.
lede: Corporate websites grew from a few pages to thousands, and suddenly dozens of people needed to edit them without breaking anything. Interwoven built software that let them work together safely. Its answer was a product called TeamSite. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, every large company had the same problem. Content management became one of the key software categories of the era.

sections.heading: Code Discipline for Web Pages
sections.body: Peng Ong founded Interwoven in 1995. He bet that websites needed the same workflow software teams used for code: versions, reviews, approvals and controlled releases. TeamSite let writers, designers and developers work side by side and publish safely, weaving many contributions into one site. It became a standard choice for big corporate websites and drew customers in media, finance and technology.

sections.heading: Law Firms, Then Autonomy
sections.body: Interwoven priced at $17 a share in October 1999 and flew high during the boom. It survived the crash and merged with iManage in 2003. That merger led it to a strong niche: document management for law firms and professional services companies. In 2009 the British software company Autonomy bought Interwoven for about $775 million. Its software lived on inside Autonomy's products.

cover.theme: women weaving on a loom (many threads, one fabric)

dek: DSL.net sold fast, always-on internet to small businesses over the copper phone lines they already had.
lede: DSL.net went looking for customers in smaller cities and towns, where it hoped to face less competition. Most small businesses there still used dial-up, or paid dearly for a dedicated line. DSL promised fast, always-on access over the copper phone lines they already had. When DSL.net filed to go public in the fall of 1999, the market was wide open, and investors were eager to fund the buildout.

sections.heading: Gear in the Central Office
sections.body: DSL.net bet that new rules from the Telecommunications Act of 1996 would let small carriers compete with the regional phone giants. It placed its own equipment in phone company central offices. It leased the copper lines to reach customers. Each new market meant buying and installing equipment before the first customer signed up. The plan needed a lot of capital and depended on cheap money.

sections.heading: Rescued, Then Absorbed
sections.body: DSL.net priced at $7.50 a share in October 1999. Within two years the DSL boom turned to bust. Capital dried up, and many competitive carriers went bankrupt. DSL.net cut back, survived on fresh financing, and kept serving business customers. In 2007 it merged into a subsidiary of MegaPath, an internet provider that already controlled it, and its public shares stopped trading.

cover.theme: a suspension bridge strung with cables (fast lines)

dek: Calico let buyers and sales teams configure complex products online and get a correct price, with no impossible combinations.
lede: Calico Commerce went from its stock offering to bankruptcy court in a little over two years. Its software guided buyers through choosing a computer server or a phone system, where many options had to fit together. The result was a correct configuration and a correct price. When Calico filed to go public in the fall of 1999, companies were rushing to sell complex products on the web. They needed tools to do it without errors.

sections.heading: Rules Behind a Product Line
sections.body: Calico bet that interactive selling would move to the web, and that configuration would be its hardest part. Its software captured the rules behind a product line, so a buyer could not order a combination that would not work. It sold mainly to technology and telecom companies with big, complex catalogs and long sales cycles. Many of its customers were Silicon Valley hardware firms.

sections.heading: Restated, Sold, Bankrupt
sections.body: Calico priced at $14 a share in October 1999. The fall of e-business spending in 2000 and 2001 hit it hard, and it restated its results for three quarters. In 2001 it sold its MarketMaker exchange business to Digital River. That December, Calico filed for Chapter 11. In February 2002 PeopleSoft bought its software and intellectual property for $5 million.

cover.theme: a cat on a balustrade (the calico)

dek: Digital Insight let community banks and credit unions offer online banking under their own names, without building it.
lede: Thousands of community banks and credit unions watched big banks build online banking and knew they could not afford to follow. Digital Insight rented it to them. Its hosted service carried each institution's own name and gave members online banking and bill payment. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, small institutions feared losing customers to big banks with better websites.

sections.heading: Your Credit Union, on Top
sections.body: Digital Insight bet that smaller financial institutions would rather rent online banking than build it. It ran the systems in its own data centers and showed them under each client's brand. Customers saw their local credit union, with no vendor in sight. The company earned recurring fees that grew as more account holders logged in. In a market full of uncertain bets, it was a steady, subscription-style business.

sections.heading: Intuit, Then NCR
sections.body: Digital Insight priced at $15 a share in September 1999. Its business kept growing after the crash, because people came to expect online banking from every bank. It bought competitors and became one of the leading providers to community banks and credit unions. In 2007 Intuit completed its purchase of Digital Insight for about $1.35 billion. In 2014 NCR bought the business from Intuit.

cover.theme: an old man in spectacles (insight, careful reckoning)
cover.artwork: Old Man with Spectacles, from Life-Sized Heads

fate: Chapter 11, 2020; later emerged as a private company
tagline: Picking the Fastest Path for Packets
dek: InterNAP sold businesses faster, more reliable internet by steering their traffic around congested public exchange points.
lede: The internet was a patchwork of networks that handed traffic to one another at crowded exchange points, where data often slowed or got lost. InterNAP built private access points wired to many major backbones. Its software picked the best path for each packet. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, businesses wanted the internet to behave as reliably as a private line.

sections.heading: A Dispatcher for Data
sections.body: Anthony Naughtin and Chris Wheeler founded InterNAP in Seattle in 1996. They bet that businesses would pay more for internet traffic that avoided congestion. InterNAP bought capacity from many backbone providers. It steered each customer's traffic over the route that performed best at that moment, like a dispatcher sending trains down the clearest track. Many of its paying customers were content and media businesses.

sections.heading: Debt, Data Centers, Chapter 11
sections.body: InterNAP priced at $20 a share in September 1999 and rose fast with the boom. The crash left it with heavy debt and falling prices. It survived, and over the following years it added data center, hosting and cloud services. The debt never went away. In 2020 the company filed for Chapter 11 and came out of the process as a private company.

cover.theme: a winter railroad yard (routing traffic down the best track)

dek: Foundry sold internet providers and data centers fast Ethernet switches that took on Cisco on speed and price.
lede: Foundry Networks arrived on the stock market with something rare for a 1999 tech offering: real profits. Networks were moving from megabits to gigabits, and the companies building them needed faster switches. Foundry made high-performance Ethernet gear that went straight at Cisco on speed and price. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, networking stocks were among the market's favorites.

sections.heading: Its Own Chips, Fast
sections.body: Bobby Johnson founded Foundry in 1996. He bet that gigabit Ethernet would spread from the backbone to the data center and the enterprise. He also bet that a focused company could build faster switches than the incumbents. Foundry designed its own chips and brought products to market fast. It sold heavily to internet providers and hosting companies that needed raw speed, and its sales grew quickly.

sections.heading: A 500 Percent First Day
sections.body: Foundry priced at $25 a share in September 1999 and closed its first day above $156, a gain of more than 500 percent. The crash cut its value sharply, but the company stayed profitable and independent for nearly a decade. In 2008 Brocade bought Foundry for about $2.6 billion, after it lowered its original offer during the financial crisis. Foundry became part of Brocade's data center networking line.

cover.theme: a blacksmith at the forge (the foundry)

dek: Keynote told companies how fast and reliably their websites loaded, by testing them from computers around the internet.
lede: A company could spend millions on a website and still not know how fast it loaded for real customers. Keynote Systems placed measurement computers across the internet and tested sites around the clock. Its public speed rankings of major sites made executives pay attention. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, slow pages were costing online businesses sales.

sections.heading: An Outside Referee
sections.body: Keynote bet that web performance would need an outside referee. Most companies had no outside measure of their own site at all. Keynote measured download times and availability from many locations, the way a customer would see them, and sold the results as a subscription. Its public index of major sites' speed gave it visibility. It turned performance into a number executives could track, compare and improve.

sections.heading: Thoma Bravo Pays $20
sections.body: Keynote priced at $14 a share in September 1999, under longtime chief executive Umang Gupta. It raised a large pile of cash during the boom and kept much of it through the downturn. It used some of that cash to buy related businesses, including mobile testing. In 2013 Thoma Bravo took Keynote private for $20 a share, about $395 million. Gupta retired as chief executive after the sale closed.

cover.theme: a woman at the piano (the keynote, finding the right pitch)

dek: eGain makes software that lets companies answer customer emails, chats and web questions faster.
lede: eGain is one of the few companies from the 1999 class still trading on Nasdaq, with its founder still in charge. It started with a simple problem. Customers had begun emailing companies in huge numbers, and most companies had no way to answer. eGain built software to sort, route and reply to that flood. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, companies selling online were discovering that every sale brought questions.

sections.heading: Sorting the Inbox
sections.body: Ashu Roy and Gunjan Sinha founded eGain in 1997. They bet that customer service would move from the phone to digital channels, and that companies would need tools to handle it at scale. eGain's software read incoming messages and sent each one to the right agent. It suggested answers from a shared knowledge base, so service teams could answer more questions faster.

sections.heading: A Founder Still in Charge
sections.body: eGain priced at $12 a share in September 1999. It rose sharply during the boom and fell hard in the crash. Unlike most of its class, it stayed independent and kept its founder in charge. It moved toward cloud software and knowledge management for customer service. More than two decades after its offering, eGain still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker EGAN.

cover.theme: wheat stacks at harvest (gain, gathered in)
cover.artwork: Stacks of Wheat (End of Day, Autumn)

dek: Vitria connected a company's separate systems so an order could move from website to warehouse to invoice on its own.
lede: Vitria became one of the most valuable software stocks of the dot-com boom by getting old computer systems to talk to each other. Large companies ran dozens of separate systems for orders, billing, inventory and customers, and those systems rarely shared anything. Vitria made software to connect them and move the work between them. When it filed to go public in the fall of 1999, companies were rushing to link their old systems to the web.

sections.heading: BusinessWare and Messaging
sections.body: JoMei Chang and Dale Skeen founded Vitria in 1994, drawing on Skeen's work in messaging systems. They bet that a company's processes, as well as its data, needed to flow across systems. Vitria's BusinessWare platform passed events between applications and modeled each step of a business process. An order could move from website to warehouse to invoice automatically. Telecom and finance were early markets.

sections.heading: Taken Private by Its Founders
sections.body: Vitria priced at $16 a share in September 1999 and soon became a boom favorite. Its sales fell as spending on integration dropped after 2000, and bigger vendors moved into its market. The founders stayed in charge the whole time. In 2007 they took Vitria private through a company they controlled. That ended its life as a public company, more than seven years after the offering.

cover.theme: a stained glass window (vitrum, glass; many panes joined into one)

dek: Lionbridge translated and tested software, websites and manuals so companies could sell in many languages.
lede: Lionbridge was built by buying translation shops around the world and joining them into one partner. Every new market a software company entered needed its own language, date formats and manuals. Lionbridge did that work, translating and testing products for global release. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, the web was making every company international overnight. Someone had to make their products speak to the world.

sections.heading: From Cottage Industry Upward
sections.body: Rory Cowan founded Lionbridge in 1996, building it partly by acquiring translation businesses worldwide. He bet that localization would grow from a small cottage industry into a core service for global companies. Lionbridge offered one partner for translation, engineering and testing across many languages, with teams in lower-cost locations. As the web spread, websites joined software as a core part of the work.

sections.heading: Bowne, Then H.I.G.
sections.body: Lionbridge priced at $10 a share in August 1999. It survived the downturn and grew by acquisition. Its biggest deal was the 2005 purchase of Bowne Global Solutions, which made it one of the largest companies in its field. It added testing and data services for technology companies. In 2017 H.I.G. Capital took Lionbridge private in a deal worth about $360 million. It remains a large localization company.

cover.theme: a lion in the mountains (the lion of Lionbridge)

tagline: One Parts List for Every Supplier
dek: Agile let manufacturers and their suppliers share one up-to-date parts list and every design change over the internet.
lede: When an electronics maker changed a design, dozens of contract manufacturers and suppliers around the world needed to know at once. Keeping all of them on the same parts list was a constant struggle. Agile Software built tools to share that product information over the internet. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, outsourced manufacturing was booming, and the chains of suppliers kept getting longer.

sections.heading: Every Change, Everywhere
sections.body: Bryan Stolle founded Agile in 1995. He bet that product information, such as bills of materials and engineering change orders, should live in one shared system every partner could reach. If a design changed, every supplier would know at once. That promised fewer errors, faster product launches and less scrap for companies that no longer built everything themselves. Electronics makers were its first big market.

sections.heading: Into Oracle's Lineup
sections.body: Agile priced at $21 a share in August 1999 and climbed steeply during the boom. Its sales fell when the technology industry cut spending after 2000. It kept growing its product lifecycle management business across more industries. In 2007 Oracle bought Agile for about $495 million and added its software to Oracle's applications for manufacturers. Agile's products lived on inside Oracle's lineup for years.

cover.theme: a leaping frog (agility and persistence)
cover.artwork: Ono no Tofu Watching a Leaping Frog

dek: Quest made tools that kept business databases fast and healthy, starting with Oracle, for the people who ran them.
lede: Quest Software's best-known tool was called TOAD, and it spread through companies one administrator at a time. Behind every big business application sat a database, and keeping it fast and healthy was a full-time job. Quest made tools for the people who did that job, beginning with Oracle databases. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, companies ran more critical systems than ever, and their administrators were stretched thin.

sections.heading: Tools From the Ground Up
sections.body: Quest was founded in 1987 in Southern California. Its bet was simple: database and application administrators needed better tools than the vendors gave them. Quest sold practical utilities, such as TOAD for Oracle developers, that solved everyday problems. Administrators bought what saved them time, and many of Quest's products spread inside companies from the ground up. It later moved its headquarters within Orange County.

sections.heading: Dozens of Deals, Then Dell
sections.body: Quest priced at $14 a share in August 1999. It kept growing after the crash, buying dozens of smaller software companies and expanding into Windows management, security and data protection. It became a large, profitable software company. In 2012, after a bidding contest with private equity firms, Dell bought Quest for about $2.4 billion. After Dell sold the business, Quest returned as an independent software company.

cover.theme: a knight on horseback (the quest)

dek: IPIX made 360-degree photos that let people look around a room online, used widely for real estate listings.
lede: IPIX's 360-degree photos grew out of robots built for dangerous places. A photo on a website was a flat rectangle. IPIX offered a spherical image you could drag to look in every direction, as if you stood in the room. The idea came from robotics work near Oak Ridge National Laboratory. When IPIX filed to go public in the summer of 1999, real estate and travel sites wanted a better way to show places.

sections.heading: Hazard Robots to Home Tours
sections.body: The company began as TeleRobotics International, founded by H. Lee Martin to build camera systems for remote work in hazardous places. Its fisheye imaging could turn two wide photos into a full sphere. IPIX bet that this immersive view would become a standard way to show homes, hotels and products online. It planned to earn a fee each time someone used an image.

sections.heading: bamboo.com, Then Bankruptcy
sections.body: IPIX priced at $18 a share in August 1999 and soon merged with bamboo.com, a rival in virtual tours for real estate. The combined company did well on listings during the boom. Losses mounted as the market fell and prices for virtual tours dropped. After years of restructuring and new products, IPIX went bankrupt in 2006. Its name lived on in later licensing.

cover.theme: a round rotunda room (a view in every direction)

dek: Tumbleweed let banks and other businesses send sensitive documents over the internet securely, with proof they arrived.
lede: Tumbleweed bet that the internet could replace the overnight courier for contracts, statements and records. Plain email was far from safe for that work. Tumbleweed made software to deliver messages and files securely, with proof of receipt. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, banks and other regulated companies were looking for a way to trust the web with sensitive documents.

sections.heading: Proof It Arrived Intact
sections.body: Jeffrey Smith and Jean-Christophe Bandini started Tumbleweed in the early 1990s. Their bet depended on one thing: making delivery secure and traceable. Tumbleweed's software encrypted messages, tracked delivery and gave both sides a record. That mattered in finance, health care and government. Those customers needed to prove that a message arrived intact, and to whom, which plain email could not do.

sections.heading: Bought by Axway
sections.body: Tumbleweed priced at $12 a share in August 1999. It soared during the boom and fell hard in the crash. It shifted toward email security and secure file transfer, sold widely to banks and government agencies, and bought several rivals. In 2008 the French software company Axway, part of Sopra Group, bought Tumbleweed. Its products became part of Axway's secure file transfer and email security lines.

cover.theme: wind-swept sands (a tumbleweed carried by the wind)

fate: Renamed Life Quotes and taken private, 2010
dek: Quotesmith let people compare insurance prices from many companies online, then buy the policy they picked.
lede: Quotesmith was comparing insurance prices years before the web arrived. Shopping for life or health insurance once meant meeting an agent who showed you a few policies of the agent's choosing. Quotesmith.com let people compare prices from many insurers on their own, then buy. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, insurance looked ripe for the price comparison already reshaping travel and books.

sections.heading: A 1984 Idea, Online
sections.body: Robert Bland founded the company in 1984 as an insurance price comparison service. The internet brought a new bet: consumers would buy insurance directly once they could see the market for themselves. Consumers were only starting to research big purchases online, so Quotesmith was early. It showed quotes from many insurers. It earned commissions as a licensed broker, and its own staff completed each sale.

sections.heading: Insure.com, Then Life Quotes
sections.body: Quotesmith priced at $11 a share in August 1999. Its shares fell fast as investors soured on internet companies, and growth came slower than hoped. It bought the Insure.com website in 2001 and later renamed itself after it. In 2009 the company sold the Insure.com and Quotesmith names and became Life Quotes, Inc. Bland led the company through every stage. It went private in 2010.

cover.theme: a blacksmith at the anvil (Quotesmith)

tagline: One Flower Shop, One Phone Number
dek: 1-800-Flowers lets people send flowers and gifts across the country with one call or click.
lede: Jim McCann bought a single flower shop in New York in 1976. He built it into a national brand around a phone number people could remember. When the web arrived, 1-800-Flowers became one of the early merchants to sell seriously online. By the summer of 1999, when it filed to go public, it was a real business with real customers, in a market crowded with promises.

sections.heading: Local Florists, National Brand
sections.body: McCann bet that people sending flowers wanted one trusted brand they could reach from anywhere. The easy phone number did that job first. A network of local florists handled delivery across the country. When the web arrived, he moved early and partnered with online services and portals. 1-800-Flowers was a familiar name before most shoppers had bought anything online at all.

sections.heading: Harry & David and Beyond
sections.body: 1-800-Flowers priced at $21 a share in August 1999. Its stock fell with the market, but the business kept selling through the downturn. Over the years it bought many gift brands, including Harry & David and Shari's Berries, and became a broad gifting company. Few retailers from the 1999 class are still public. 1-800-Flowers still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker FLWS.

cover.theme: a bouquet of flowers
cover.artwork: Bouquet of Flowers in an Earthenware Vase

fate: Taken private by Vector Capital and Francisco Partners, 2006 (~$151M)
dek: WatchGuard sells simple firewall boxes that protect small and mid-sized businesses, installed and managed by local resellers.
lede: WatchGuard's firewall came in a bright red box called the Firebox, and it became a familiar sight in small server closets. The company started in Seattle as Seattle Software Labs. Small businesses were connecting to the internet full time and becoming easy targets. The Firebox stood guard between their network and the outside world. When WatchGuard filed to go public in the summer of 1999, network security was moving into every office.

sections.heading: Security a Reseller Could Install
sections.body: WatchGuard bet that small and mid-sized companies needed serious network security but could not afford complex systems or expert staff. It built firewalls into simple appliances that resellers could install and manage. It also sold subscriptions for updates and services. The box got WatchGuard in the door. Each one then brought in recurring revenue for as long as the customer kept it.

sections.heading: Private, and Still in Seattle
sections.body: WatchGuard priced at $13 a share in July 1999. It survived the crash but struggled to grow profitably as competition increased. In 2006 Vector Capital and Francisco Partners took it private for about $151 million. As a private company it kept growing into wireless, endpoint and identity security. Vector Capital became its majority owner in 2022, and WatchGuard is still based in Seattle.

cover.theme: an old watchtower (on guard)

dek: Net2Phone let people make cheap long distance calls over the internet, first from computers and later from regular phones.
lede: A call from New York to India could cost more than a dollar a minute. Net2Phone let people make that call over the internet for a fraction of the price. It was spun out of IDT, the discount long distance carrier. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, internet telephony was a young idea, and Net2Phone was one of its best-known names.

sections.heading: IDT's Idea, Moved Online
sections.body: Howard Jonas built IDT by selling cheap international calling. Net2Phone took the same idea to the internet, and it moved early. The bet was that voice would move onto data networks, where calls cost far less to carry. Net2Phone started with calls from a PC to a regular phone. Then it sold its service through partners, devices and businesses around the world.

sections.heading: AT&T In, IDT Back
sections.body: Net2Phone priced at $15 a share in July 1999 and rose sharply in the months after. In 2000 AT&T took a large stake in the company. As internet calling became common and prices fell, Net2Phone struggled to make money from it. In 2006 IDT bought back the shares it did not already own. The service carried on under IDT for years after the deal.

cover.theme: a steamship crossing the sea (calls across the ocean)
cover.artwork: Arrival and Departure of an American Steamship (Amerikakoku jokisha orai)

dek: drugstore.com delivered vitamins, shampoo, cold medicine and prescriptions to the door, so customers could skip the pharmacy trip.
lede: drugstore.com wanted to move the corner pharmacy online, from vitamins and shampoo to prescriptions, all delivered to the door. Famous investors backed it, including Amazon. Former Microsoft executive Peter Neupert ran it. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, online retail was the market's favorite story. Drugstore goods seemed perfect for the web, because people buy them again and again.

sections.heading: Rite Aid and Repeat Buyers
sections.body: drugstore.com bet that the drugstore, with its frequent, routine purchases, would move online once ordering got easy. Customers would save trips and gain privacy. drugstore.com would win loyal repeat buyers. It formed a partnership with Rite Aid to handle prescriptions. It spent heavily on marketing to build its brand fast. Amazon, an early investor, was a close partner in its first years.

sections.heading: Walgreens Buys, Then Closes
sections.body: drugstore.com priced at $18 a share in July 1999. It lost large sums for years, because shipping low-priced goods cost so much. Over time it focused on beauty and health products, bought Beauty.com, and reached hundreds of millions of dollars in yearly sales. In 2011 Walgreens bought the company for about $409 million. Five years later, in 2016, Walgreens shut the site down.

cover.theme: an old apothecary storefront

fate: Sold its businesses to a Comcast-led venture and SeaChange, 2005
tagline: Email on the Living Room TV
dek: Liberate made software that put email, shopping and interactive shows on cable TV boxes.
lede: Liberate Technologies grew out of Oracle's network computer effort and bet that the internet would arrive through the television. Its software ran on cable set-top boxes. It promised email, shopping and interactive programs in the living room. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, cable companies were promising interactive TV everywhere. Liberate wanted to be the software inside every one of those boxes.

sections.heading: A Platform Microsoft Didn't Control
sections.body: Liberate bet that cable operators would need a standard software platform for interactive television. They would want one that Microsoft did not control. Liberate offered that platform and signed deals with major cable and telecom companies around the world, often granting them warrants in return. The warrants gave each partner a stake in Liberate's success. If interactive TV took off, Liberate would sit inside millions of homes.

sections.heading: Interactive TV Arrives Late
sections.body: Liberate priced at $16 a share in July 1999 and became one of the most valuable software companies of the boom. Interactive TV came far more slowly than promised, and the company later restated revenue. In 2005 it sold its North American business to a venture led by Comcast. It sold its international business to SeaChange. Then it paid its remaining cash out to shareholders.

cover.theme: cranes on a snowy pine (poised for flight, liberation)

dek: Engage tracked what anonymous web users did, so advertisers could show each person ads that matched their interests.
lede: Engage built anonymous profiles of what people did online, so it could show each visitor ads more likely to match their interests. It was one of the companies in CMGI's sprawling internet empire. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, online advertising was growing fast. Targeting was the idea everyone wanted to own. Four years later, Engage was in bankruptcy court.

sections.heading: Interest Groups for Advertisers
sections.body: Engage bet that the web could make advertising far more precise than print or television. It collected anonymous behavior data across many sites and sorted visitors into interest groups. Advertisers could buy an audience instead of a page. Engage paired that data with ad networks and ad-serving software, including AdKnowledge and Flycast, which CMGI folded into it. The goal was a full system for online marketing.

sections.heading: CMGI Walks Away
sections.body: Engage priced at $15 a share in July 1999 and became a high-flying CMGI stock. When the online ad market collapsed in 2000 and 2001, revenue fell hard and losses mounted. Engage sold AdKnowledge in 2001. CMGI gave up its stake in 2002. In 2003 Engage filed for Chapter 11 and agreed to sell its remaining assets to Scene7 for $1.2 million.

cover.theme: a fan raised as a target (aiming at the audience)
cover.artwork: Lady Tamamushi raising a fan target

dek: ATG made software that let big retailers run online stores that remembered each shopper and tailored what they saw.
lede: Art Technology Group started in Cambridge as a small consulting firm with an artful name, and ended up running the online stores of big brands. Its software let those stores remember each customer and tailor what they saw. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, big brands were racing to sell on the web. ATG offered them a serious platform for doing it.

sections.heading: Dynamo and the MIT Founders
sections.body: Jeet Singh and Joe Chung, both with roots at MIT, founded ATG in 1991. They bet that big online businesses would need a powerful platform built for personalization, a step beyond a catalog and a cart. ATG's Dynamo software showed each visitor different products and offers based on that visitor's behavior. That made it popular with big retailers and media companies.

sections.heading: A Billion From Oracle
sections.body: ATG priced at $12 a share in July 1999 and became one of the hottest software stocks of the boom. The crash hit it hard and forced deep cuts. The company recovered as big retailers kept spending on online sales. Its commerce platform became a common choice for major brands. In 2011, nearly twelve years after its offering, Oracle bought ATG for about $1 billion.

cover.theme: an artist in his studio (the art in Art Technology Group)

tagline: Freed From Lucent, Betting on DSL
dek: Paradyne made the DSL gear that let phone companies send fast data over the copper lines already in place.
lede: Paradyne made data communications equipment for decades, first on its own and then as part of AT&T and Lucent. Then an investment firm bought it and set it loose on DSL, the technology for sending broadband over ordinary copper phone lines. Paradyne became an early leader. When it filed to go public in the summer of 1999, phone companies were rushing to sell DSL, and Paradyne's gear sat at the heart of many deployments.

sections.heading: Faster Than a Giant Parent
sections.body: Texas Pacific Group bought Paradyne from Lucent in 1996. The bet was that a focused company could move faster than a giant parent. Paradyne pushed its broadband access products, which let carriers reuse the copper already running into homes and offices. Fast data over old wires promised to turn the phone network into a broadband network without digging new lines.

sections.heading: Swapped for Zhone Stock
sections.body: Paradyne priced at $17 a share in July 1999 and soared during the DSL boom. When many young DSL carriers failed in 2000 and 2001, demand for its equipment fell sharply. The company cut costs and kept selling broadband access gear to carriers. In 2005 Zhone Technologies bought Paradyne in an all-stock deal worth about $180 million. Its gear lived on in Zhone's broadband access line.

cover.theme: a storm over the land (lightning in the copper)
